facts.text: Ol' Dirty Bastard borrowed this movie's name for his 1995 debut album, Return to the 36 Chambers: The Dirty Version. Brooklyn Zoo and Shimmy Shimmy Ya came out of it.
Gordon Liu played the serious monk San Te in the first film. Here he's a fake monk and a comic con man. Fans call it a very different tone.
Director Lau Kar-leung also choreographed all three 36th Chamber films. His father Lau Cham trained under a student of folk hero Wong Fei-hung.
Gordon Liu is the adopted brother of the film's director, Lau Kar-leung. He took the Liu surname out of respect for his teacher, Hung Gar master Lau Cham.
The film was released in Hong Kong on August 24, 1980. Screenwriter Ni Kuang wrote it, and Mona Fong and Run Run Shaw produced it.
Gordon Liu later played two roles in the Kill Bill films: Johnny Mo and the white-haired master Pai Mei.
Hou Hsiao trained in Chinese opera and says Yuen Wah deserves the title of best acrobat from those schools, not him.
Kwon Yeong-moon, who appears here, later taught tae kwon do to Sylvester Stallone and Muhammad Ali. He also starred in the cult film Miami Connection.
Instead of kung fu lessons, our hero is ordered to build bamboo scaffolding, and that labor teaches him the skills. Critics love the idea.
Lung-Wei Wang, who plays the boss, usually played villains. He was also in Five Deadly Venoms.
The trilogy ended with Disciples of the 36th Chamber in 1985, the same year Shaw Brothers stopped making films.
Gordon Liu started as a stuntman, then became a martial arts instructor. Fans picture him as the Kung-Fu Monk, and he's often a bald monk.
Lau Kar-leung only wrote four screenplays, all for films he directed. This wasn't one of them. Ni Kuang wrote it.
